spanish_col.markdown:
their wives, et cetera. And if someone speaks, he [the drunkard] thinks [that person] is whispering something about him. And if somebody laughs, he thinks that he himself is the butt of the joke. And so he quarrels with everybody without any rhyme or reason. He does this because he is unhinged by the wine.

And if the one who gets drunk is a woman, she falls right away on the floor, curling up in a ball. And sometimes she stretches her legs out on that floor. If she is really drunk, she messes up her hair. And she is all disheveled and sleeps with her hair all messed up, et cetera.

Of all these types of drunkards mentioned above, they said that [type of] drunkard was his own rabbit[^10] or the particular condition of his own drunkenness or the particular demon that had entered into him.

If some drunkard fell off a cliff or killed himself, they would say, “He has ‘rabbit-ted’ himself.” Because there are different kinds of wine, and [each] elicits different kinds of drunkards, they called [wine] _centzontotochti_, that is, “four hundred rabbits,” as if to say that it makes infinite kinds of drunkards. Moreover, they said that when the sign Ome Tochtli arrived, they would celebrate a festival for the principal god of the gods of wine, 


[^10]: “That [type of] . . . rabbit”: _que aquel borracho era su conejo_.

nor chastise his tongue. No one could force him to recant. He thought himself superior, better than others.

Indistinct was his speech. What did he say? He was as if stirred, and his words bubbled up and burst forth. It was as if he argued, harangued, enforced silence, and drove all people away, put them to flight, numbed them with terror, visited them with afflictions, made them shrink with fright, and assailed them with his words.

It seemed that he disgusted others, and did not inquire what they said. Wherever they may have spoken, or undertaken something, he seemed to make little of it and kick it aside. But when he had drunk nothing, he seemed to be dumb, one who whispered, fearful of people, quite frightened.

For all this he excused himself by saying: “It is because I no longer knew what I said; for I was drunk. The wine had taken effect upon me; I was overwrought.”

And another drunkard was very suspicious. He misunderstood; not as things were did he hear them. Often he blamed his wife. If anyone only looked at her, he then said to him: “Why dost thou make eyes at my wife?” Then he gave rise
